title: Optimal Quantum Eigenvalue Transformation via Linear Combinations of Hermitian Matrices
authors: Yanqiao Wang, Yixuan Liang, Hongjia Chen, Jin-Peng Liu
abstract: We discover two complementary linear-combination-of-Hermitian-matrices (LCHM) formulations to achieve a general non-normal matrix eigenvalue transformation $g(A)$. Firstly, for $A=L+\mathrm{i} H$ with Hermitian $L$ and $H$, the vanilla LCHM formula represents $g(A)$ as a kernel integral of $g(\mathrm{i}(H+kL))$, and it contains linear-combination-of-Hamiltonian-simulation (LCHS) [An, Liu, Lin, Phys. Rev. Lett. 2023] as the special case for matrix exponentials. Secondly, for the angular Hermitian $X_θ= \cosθL+\sinθH$, the Weyl LCHM formula expresses $g(A)$ via integrating $g(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}θ} (X_θ\pm\mathrm{i}(I-X_θ^2)^{1/2}))$. For the matrix power $g(A)=A^m$, the Fourier projection of Weyl LCHM gives \[ A^m=\frac{2}π\int_0^π\text{e}^{\text{i} mθ}T_m(X_θ) \text{d}θ= \frac{2}{N}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1} \text{e}^{\text{i} mθ_j}T_m(X_{θ_j}),\quadθ_j=\frac{πj}{N},\quad \text{for every } N>m \] with Chebyshev polynomial of Hermitian $T_m(X_θ)$ and $N$ samples. The discrete formula is exact, introduces no truncation and angular quadrature error, and offers $\mathcal{O}(1)$ post-selection weights.   LCHM formulas lead to new quantum eigenvalue transformation (QET) algorithms. For a degree-$d$ polynomial $p_d(A)$ on $|ψ\rangle$, our QET algorithm can achieve optimal $Θ(d)$ circuit depth and optimal $\mathcal{O}(||p_d||_{\infty}/||p_d(A)|ψ\rangle||)$ post-selection repetitions. LCHM-based QETs unify various quantum linear algebraic problems with near-optimal $\mathcal{\widetilde O}(d\log(d/ε))$ Clifford$+T$ gates, including driven ODEs (reduced to standard LCHS), iterative methods, resolvents, $\log(I+A)$, $(λI+A)^ν$, Sign and ReLU transforms, and Faber approximation on noncircular domains.
summary: This paper introduces Linear Combination of Hermitian Matrices (LCHM) formulations to efficiently compute functions of general, non-normal matrices $g(A)$ in the quantum domain. By developing both Vanilla and Weyl LCHM methods, the authors achieve optimal circuit depth for various quantum linear algebraic tasks. This work provides a powerful theoretical framework for advancing quantum simulation beyond standard Hermitian models.
main_problem: The central problem is developing optimal quantum eigenvalue transformation (QET) algorithms for general non-normal matrices, which surpasses the capabilities of standard singular value transformations.
main_result: The paper introduces Linear Combination of Hermitian Matrices (LCHM) formulations that achieve near-optimal circuit depth ($\Theta(d)$) and provide exact discrete formulas for matrix powers using Fourier projection techniques.
method: Two complementary LCHM methods—Vanilla and Weyl—are developed to map the general non-normal function $g(A)$ onto integrals or sums involving Hermitian matrices. These are then implemented into quantum circuits achieving optimal gate complexity.
model_or_system: The theory applies to computing functions $g(A)$ of a general matrix $A$, where $A$ is decomposed using its Hermitian and anti-Hermitian parts ($L, H$). The analysis often uses weighted-shift matrices as test cases to prove quantum advantage.
key_observables: Quantum query complexity, circuit depth ($\Theta(d)$), post-selection repetition count, and operator-norm error bounds ($\epsilon_{	ext{circ}}, \epsilon_{	ext{app}}$).
important_parameters: The degree of the polynomial ($d$), the numerical radius $w(A)$, and approximation parameters like $\epsilon$ or sampling size $N$.
main_assumptions: The methods rely on decomposing $A$ into Hermitian components and assume conditions (like a uniform numerical-radius gap) are met to demonstrate exponential quantum advantage.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the mathematical necessity of LCHM over standard techniques, detailing the Vanilla and Weyl formulations for $g(A)$, deriving exact discrete formulas (e.g., for $A^m$), and concluding with the complexity analysis of the resulting QET algorithms.
why_interesting: The development of robust, near-optimal quantum linear algebra tools like LCHM is crucial for implementing complex quantum simulations involving non-Hermitian Hamiltonians or time evolution operators that cannot be easily mapped to standard Hermitian forms.
